1.1 Background information: Spatial Data
The following book is aimed as a starting guide to get started with spatial and ecological data for statistical analyses. Most steps are kept simple for this tutorial but I’ve highlighted points where more advanced processing is usually necessary.

title: 1  Introduction to spatial ecology
text:
1.1.1 Types of spatial phenomena

Spatial phenomena can generally be thought of as either discrete objects with clear boundaries or as a continuous phenomena that can be observed everywhere, but that do not have natural boundaries. Discrete spatial objects may refer to a river, road, country, town, or a research site. Examples of continuous phenomena, or “spatial fields”, include elevation, temperature, and air quality.
- quote from https://rspatial.org/spatial/2-spatialdata.html

We distinguish these continuous and discrete spatial phenomena using different object types (vector, raster). Both of these include information on the “geometry” (also referred to as “geom”) or “shape” of the object, and additional data “attributes”. The geometry usually represents a set of coordinates (in pairs: x,y).
The most important data types are: vectors and rasters

discrete variables - vector datacontinuous variables - raster data



points

the simplest case with only one coordinate-pair per point, but it can have multiple associated variables (“attributes”), such as environmental measurements or species presence/absence data.
there are also multi-point classes where multiple points have been combined into a structure with a single attribute record, for example the places where a single species has been recorded as present.

lines (or networks)

lines (or more correctly: poly-lines) can represent single lines or a connected series of line segments (e.g., a river or single tributaries inside the river).
They are represented as ordered set of coordinates that connect points - this is also what distinguishes them from points.
Networks contain additional information about the lines like, for example, the flow, connectivity, distance, direction of a river.

polygons

represent a set of closed poly-lines where the last coordinate pair is identical with the first coordinate pair.
Polygons can have holes (e.g., to show a lake in a terrestrial landscape).
There are some rules that make polygons valid and it’s always good to check the validity because spatial data is often transformed and projected and combined with other data, thereby deforming the spatial objects and potentially introducing issues. One of the rules is that polygons must not self-intersect.
A set of polygons can be combined to a multi-polygon, e.g., when looking at the spatially disjunct distribution range of a species, all polygons where the species occurs can be combined to a multi-polygon with gaps between polygons.





rasters represent continuous phenomena split up into equally-sized rectangles (“grid cells”). Each cell has one or more attributes (or variables) associated with it (can also be missing values).
A single cell usually represents the average (mean, median) of all values inside the grid cell, but it’s possible to calculate any type of summary statistics during rasterization of continuous data. Sometimes it’s even the measured value at the centre of the cell.
raster objects do not explicitly store the geometry data as coordinates. Rather, the grid is implicitly set by indicating the spatial extent and number of rows and columns which divide the area. Given these information, the size of each cell can be calculated.
Rasters can be interpreted as an efficient way to store polygons that form a regular grid without having to save their coordinates - these can be easily computed since the grid is structured. This decreases computation time and memory storage of data.






1.1.2 R software for spatial data
Originally there were two packages which have been replaced by more recent developed ones. The two packages were raster for rasters and sp for vectors. These packages are not maintained anymore. Newer (and better) libraries are terra for raster and vectors and sf for vectors. Both libraries overlap in their application but they handle spatial information in very different ways. While terra uses a rather complex data structure, sf is easier to use and works perfectly within the tidyverse, including native support for sf within ggplot2.

terrasfterra-sf interactions


replaces both outdated libraries: sp and raster. The extension library tidyterra enables compatibility with tidyverse-functions for handling and manipulation (including piping).

Vector data:

Data classes: SpatVector
File format: shapefile (.shp) (use terra::vect() to read in or convert foreign objects to SpatVector))
Extract data: terra::as.data.frame(shp)
Extract data with coordinates: terra::as.data.frame(shp, xy = TRUE)
requires the library tidyterra to use tidyverse operations, otherwise use base-R language.
Modifying vectors in terra: https://rspatial.org/spatial/7-vectmanip.html

Raster data:

Data class: SpatRaster
file format: GeoTIFF, ESRI, ENVI, ERDAS (use terra::rast() to load or convert foreign objects to raster)
Extract data: terra::values(tif)
Extract data with cell-centroid coordinates: terra::as.data.frame(tif, xy = TRUE)
rasters can be “stacked” to a single data object with multiple layers using: c(raster1, raster2, raster3)
can easily be created from scratch (using rast()) with additional arguments: xmin, nrow, ncol, and/or crs; or “rasterized” using a template and a dataframe with coordinates using rasterize(data, template)
Modifying rasters in terra: https://rspatial.org/spatial/8-rastermanip.html#modifying-a-spatraster-object




sf replaces the outdated libraries: sp, rgdal, rgeos and is also a new way of representing geo-spatial data as “simple features”. Features are objects in the real world (for example: an area, a building, an individual organism recorded in the a certain place and time). These features have geometries describing the location of the feature in the real world, and attributes associated with it (for examples: traits measured). It works directly with tidyverse functions for handling and manipulation. It also provides access to Google’s spherical geometry library (s2) to fast and accurate computations on non-planar geometries. this is enabled by default for geographic (latitude/longitude) coordinate systems.
More information: https://r.geocompx.org/spatial-class#intro-sf

Vector data:

Data class: sf and data.frame
file format: shapefile (.shp) (use st_read() to load)
convert foreign objects to an sf object with: st_as_sf()
data can be extracted by removing the geometry column with st_drop_geometry()




https://r.geocompx.org/raster-vector
It is not always easy to handle both sf and terra objects together but it is often necessary, for example when downloading external data. terra can use the information provided in sf objects to work with rasters, for example when extracting raster-values for certain sf-geometries.
Similarly, sf can use information provided from raster objects to modify the sf object.

sf::st_transform(sf, st_crs(raster)) will match the CRS of the sf to the one from the raster.
terra::crop(raster, sf) will crop the raster to the extent of the sf object
terra::mask(raster, sf) will set the outside values of the bounds of the sf object to NA in the raster
terra::extract(raster, sf, exact = TRUE) will extract the values from the raster for the points, lines, or polygons in the sf object
This can be a bit slow but there is the library extactextract which speeds things up significantly: https://github.com/isciences/exactextractr
converting a raster to a vector (and converting it to sf) is called “vectorization” and can be done with:
terra::as.polygons(raster) %>% sf::st_as_sf() for polygons,
terra::as.points(raster) %>% sf::st_as_sf() for points, or
terra::as.contour(raster) %>% sf::st_as_sf() for lines






1.1.3 Coordinate Reference Systems (CRS)
CRS are an essential aspect of spatial data as it indicates the reference point of the coordinate system used: A location of (3, 10) cannot be interpreted without knowledge where the point of origin (0, 0) is located, and knowledge about the unit of the coordinates (meters, feet, miles, kilometres, degrees) of the distance between the point and the origin. Below I explain the parameters we need to get to our CRS.

1.1.3.1 Geographical coordinates - Spherical CRS

The earth has an irregular spheroid-like shape. The natural coordinate reference system for geographic data is longitude/latitude. This is an angular coordinate reference system. The latitude 𝜙 (phi) of a point is the angle between the equatorial plane and the line that passes through a point and the center of the Earth. Longitude 𝜆 (lambda) is the angle from a reference meridian (lines of constant longitude) to a meridian that passes through the point.
- quote from https://rspatial.org/spatial/6-crs.html

Meaning that we need to know the angles when interpreting latitude/longitude coordinates. Since we cannot measure these angles, we need to estimate them from a model of Earth’s shape (“datum”). Examples are:

Spheroid datum:

Describes Earth as a sphere that is flattened at the poles and enlarged at the equator

WGS84 (World Geodetic System 1984)

Describes Earth’s surface with more complexity
Is used in GPS
It’s origin (0, 0) is at the Earth’s centre of mass (< 2 cm uncertainty): slightly (102 m) east of the Greenwich meridian at the equator.
CRS: "EPSG:4326"

Local datums

record more precisely locations for a single country or region




1.1.3.2 Projections - Making Earth planar
Geographic coordinates are a three dimensional system (latitude, longitude, altitude; x, y, z) but in cartography we need to transform it into a two dimensional plane to visualize a map. It also makes certain calculations calculations easier. Planar CRS are referred to as “projections”.
It is impossible to transform a 3D object into a 2D representation without introducing distortions. This means we have to make an important consideration before choosing a projection: Do we want to keep the scale (i.e., area) constant or the shape (i.e., distances) as they are seen on a globe? Some projections are global, others are only for small areas. There is no one-size-fits-all solution to all projections since each has it’s own trade-offs. Some projections approximate both, equal-area and conformal shape, e.g., UTM for smaller areas and Lambert Equal Area for larger areas.
Here are some images of projections to familiarize yourself with what it does: all projection images
Luckily, there are useful tools that let us easily get the best projection for our study area and application: https://projectionwizard.org/
Just crop the map to the study area, chose whether you want equal-area or equal-distance (shape) and copy the projection string in prj or wkt format. Both of those can be read by R.


1.1.3.3 Additional parameters of planar CRS
A planar CRS is defined by 1) a projection 2) a datum 3) parameters based on projection. R recognizes the notation of the additional parameters in forms of multiple systems:

if WGS84-datum based: PROJ.4 notation still works but is not fully supported any more
EPSG (European Petroleum Survey Group) Codes: Unique ID to identify a CRS. The ID has been assigned for most commonly used CRS. For example, WGS84 is EPSG:4326.
https://epsg.io/4326
Well-Known-Text (wtk) : a mark-up language fore representing vector geometry objects. It is the open standard format for describing CRSs developed by the Open Geospatial Consortium (OGC)
https://docs.ogc.org/is/18-010r7/18-010r7.html



1.1.3.4 Projecting in R

terra::project(vector, crs) spatial vectors can be easily transformed to another projection.
rasters should not be projected if it can be avoided since it would involve changing the coordinates of pixels separately. Rather, there is a workaround:

Create a template SpatRaster with the desired geometry created via rast()
rasters require equal-area projections to assure the grid cells are of the same size and therefore comparable to each other.

The functions terra::crs() and sf::st_crs() do not alter the CRS. they simply print the one that was supplied or re-label the CRS in the data object. They do not transform the data themselves.







TipIs it always necessary to project?



R’s ability to work with lat/lon CRSs has substantially improved recently with sf and terra.
sf has now an integration with the S2 spherical geometry engine from Google and the user can chose whether they want to use S2 or GEOS via the function: sf::sf_use_s2(FALSE). S2 is enabled by default and GEOS is always used for projected data and data with no CRS. Spherical CRS can be used with S2 enabled.
Calculations on properly projected CRSs and geographic (lat/lon) CRS produce similarly accurate results. Using S2 can thus be used if an appropiate planar projection can not be found (as may be the case over large areas or when doing calculations based on area AND on distance).

1.2 Background Information: Species occurrence data
We will access the Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF) (https://www.gbif.org/) to get some species occurrence data within R. This makes the occurrence download reproducible and sharable with others.






ImportantNotes on data quality for statistical analyses



Data on GBIF has multiple sources and has not been collected in a structured way. Therefore, the assumption for most statistical models, that the data captures a representative random sample of the true world, is not met. This is because it favors certain spatial areas and temporal time spans over others. This has natural causes that lie in the limitations of humans to collect data without these spatial and temporal “biases”.
Examples for such biases and possible ways to tackle them can be found in the review I linked earlier (https://ecoevorxiv.org/repository/view/12816/).


We will keep it simple for now and only apply basic data-cleaning methods to improve the data quality a bit. Check out the library coordinateCleaner for more ways to remove data points with errors.

1.2.1 Accessing GBIF
First we need to set up our GBIF credentials in R. Run the code below and then edit the file that opens (.Renviron). We need to enter the variables GBIF_USER, GBIF_PWD, GBIF_EMAIL (see example below), then save the file and restart the R session (in the menu bar on top, click ‘Session’ and then ‘Restart R’)

usethis::edit_r_environ()

Example variable enties to .Renviron:
GBIF_USER="YOUR USER NAME"
GBIF_PWD="YOUR_PASSWORD"
GBIF_EMAIL="YOUR_EMAIL_ADDRESS"
Now we are set up. Let’s start!

2.0.1 Section 1: Libraries
Make sure you have read the part about projections and CRS from the introduction page before starting.
We will start our code by first ensuring that our R environment and memory is clean and empty, and then we will install and load R libraries (Section 1) and set up variables in R for file paths or frequently used objects (Section 2).
I wrote a function that I use in most of my projects to download and load R libraries. Usually I would save the function into it’s own R-script and load it using the source() function. However, for the purporse of this tutorial it’s best to see the actual function and try to understand what it does. It’s generally a good idea to do that for functions that have not been written by yourself in R. While the function I wrote is useful when you work a lot in R, you can also do the same job by hand using multiple lines of code: install.packages(“package1”), install.packages(“package2”), …, library(package1), library(package2), and so on.
# ------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# 1. Install packages if not already installed and load them
# ------------------------------------------------------------------- #

install_if_missing <-
  function(packages) {
    missing <-
      packages[!packages %in% rownames(installed.packages())]

    # first install the missing libraries
    if (length(missing) > 0) {
      install.packages(
        missing,
        repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org"
      )
    }
    # now load the libraries into our active R session
    x <- suppressPackageStartupMessages(
      lapply(packages, require, character.only = TRUE)
    )
    rm(x)
  }
library(here)

2.1 1. Retrieving data for plotting a map
There are many software tools for creating maps in R. It’s possible to create interactive .html maps using R libraries such as tmap or leaflet. For printing it’s better to keep the maps static (non-interactive). We will start with that and if you want to make them interactive, feel free to do it in addition!
geodata is a fantastic library that combines the access to different kinds of geospatial datasets under one hood. You can check out all the data it has here: https://rspatial.github.io/geodata/
In order to use it most efficiently, we need to assign a path on your computer where the geodata should be downloaded to. Here we will save it to the sub-folder data and create another sub-folder named geodata: results/geodata

if (!dir.exists(path_geodata)) {
  dir.create(path_geodata, recursive = TRUE)
}


geodata_path(here(path_geodata))


2.1.1 Downloading data
We will start simple by downloading the administrative borders of a country using the r package geodata. We can use the geodata::gadm() function (or simply gadm()) to retrieve administrative border for Madagascar, it’s regions, districts and communes.
The default return class of the gadm() function is a SpatVector (spatial vector; the native format of the library terra).

# administrative level 3: communes
# (includes level 0:country, level 1:region, level 2:district)
# discrete variable: vector

# download the data to the geodata_path location
geodata::gadm("MDG", level = 3)



2.1.2 Loading data into R
The file format of the administrative borders is already an object specifically for R (.rds). It’s a fast way of storing R objects while conserving all kinds of parameters about the data, like it’s class or types of columns.

# load the data from file (SpatVector)
# read administrative borders:
adm3 <-
  readRDS(here(path_geodata, "gadm", "gadm41_MDG_3_pk.rds")) %>%
  select("NAME_1", "NAME_2", "NAME_3")

Make a map with tmap that can be zoomed in and out

  tm_borders(fill = "NAME_1") +
  tm_text("NAME_3")






Let’s look at different projections and how they change the shape of Madagascar. Below we are comparing WGS84 (the GPS standard in latitude and longitude), equal-area Behrmann projection (global, in Meters), and equal-area projection centered on Madagascar (by projectionwizard.org)
tmap_mode(mode = "plot")
par(mfrow = c(3,1))

# WGS 84 - lat/long
tm_shape(adm3, component.autoscale = FALSE) +
  tm_borders() +
  tm_compass(position = c("left", "top")) +
  tm_scalebar(breaks = c(0, 15, 30), text.size = 1) +
  tm_minimap(height = 3, width = 3)

# Behrman planar projection - meters
tm_shape(adm3) +
  tm_borders() +
  tm_crs(wkt_behrm) +
  tm_compass(position = c("left", "top")) +
  tm_scalebar(breaks = c(0, 15, 30), text.size = 1) +
  tm_minimap(height = 3, width = 3)

# projectionwizard: equal area, centered on MDG

  tm_borders() +
  tm_crs(wkt_mda) +
  tm_compass(position = c("left", "top")) +
  tm_scalebar(breaks = c(0, 15, 30), text.size = 1) +
  tm_minimap(height = 3, width = 3)

title: 3  Download GBIF data
text:
3.1 Download data from GBIF
Let’s check out some data on GBIF. Here we will download all occurrences of Tracheophytes (vascular plants) in Madagascar that are herbarium specimens, human observations or observations. This will likely be a big download. Feel free to reduce it further with smaller groups of organisms for testing things.

taxon_key <- name_backbone("Tracheophyta")$usageKey
country_code <- "MG"
basis_of_record <- c('PRESERVED_SPECIMEN', 'HUMAN OBSERVATION', 'OBSERVATION')

We use the function occ_download() to prepare big downloads in the background. You will be notified when the download is ready and you can access it later through your user-account via gbif.org The download will be a .zip folder with a .csv inside. Unzip the folder and place the .csv in your data folder.

occ_download(
  pred("country", country_code),
  pred_in("basisOfRecord", basis_of_record),
  pred("taxonKey", taxon_key),
  pred("hasCoordinate", TRUE),
  pred("hasGeospatialIssue", FALSE),
  format = "SIMPLE_CSV"
)

3.2 Pre-process the GBIF data
Let’s apply some first filter on our data to reduce computing time later. There is some informative metadata included in the table that we got from GBIF and we will use them to apply a first quality filter on the data.
At the same time, we will reduce the number of columns in the dataset because we do not need them all for our purpose.

dat <-
  dl %>%
  # select only some columns:
  dplyr::select(
    species,
    decimalLongitude,
    decimalLatitude,
    countryCode,
    gbifID,
    taxonRank,
    genus,
    family,
    order,
    coordinateUncertaintyInMeters,
    year,
    basisOfRecord,
    stateProvince) %>%
  # remove entries with missing lat or lon data:
  filter(!is.na(decimalLongitude)) %>%
  filter(!is.na(decimalLatitude)) %>%
  # remove entries that have not been identify at least to family level
  filter(!is.na(family)) %>%
  # remove coordinates that are known to have low precision
  filter(coordinateUncertaintyInMeters <= 50000 | is.na(coordinateUncertaintyInMeters)) %>%
  select(!coordinateUncertaintyInMeters) %>%
  # remove duplicates in the data frame
  distinct() %>%
  # factors are usually faster to calculate with than charaters. We will transform some columns from character to factor:
  mutate(
    countryCode = as.factor(countryCode),
    taxonRank = as.factor(taxonRank),
    genus = as.factor(genus),
    family = as.factor(family),
    order = as.factor(order),
    basisOfRecord = as.factor(basisOfRecord),
    stateProvince = as.factor(stateProvince)
  )

4.0.1 Section 1: Libraries
Make sure you have read the part about projections and CRS from the introduction page before starting.
We will start our code by first ensuring that our R environment and memory is clean and empty, and then we will install and load R libraries (Section 1) and set up variables in R for file paths or frequently used objects (Section 2).
I wrote a function that I use in most of my projects to download and load R libraries. Usually I would save the function into it’s own R-script and load it using the source() function. However, for the purporse of this tutorial it’s best to see the actual function and try to understand what it does. It’s generally a good idea to do that for functions that have not been written by yourself in R. While the function I wrote is useful when you work a lot in R, you can also do the same job by hand using multiple lines of code: install.packages(“package1”), install.packages(“package2”), …, library(package1), library(package2), and so on.
# ------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# 1. Install packages if not already installed and load them
# ------------------------------------------------------------------- #

install_if_missing <-
  function(packages) {
    missing <-
      packages[!packages %in% rownames(installed.packages())]

    # first install the missing libraries
    if (length(missing) > 0) {
      install.packages(
        missing,
        repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org"
      )
    }
    # now load the libraries into our active R session
    x <- suppressPackageStartupMessages(
      lapply(packages, require, character.only = TRUE)
    )
    rm(x)
  }
# list all packages needed for the code
package_list <-
  c(
    "here",
    "dplyr",
    "ggplot2",
    "sf",
    "terra",
    "tidyterra",
    "geodata",
    "skimr",
    "cowplot",
    "tmap"
  )
# run the function - may require your input in the console
install_if_missing(package_list)

# delete the list object from our r environment
rm(package_list)

4.1 Downloading environmental data
Let’s download some environmental data. 1) We will download elevation 2) We will get a couple of soil content variables from isda african soil database 3) We will download some climate data from worldclim (annual temperature, annual precipitation, precipitation seasonality) 4) We will download human footprint data.

## 1. elevation (continuos variable - SpatRaster)
geodata::elevation_30s("MDG")

## 2. african soil data (continuos variable - SpatRaster)
geodata::soil_af_isda(
  var = c(
    "oc", # organic carbon (g kg^-1)
    "c.tot", # total carbon (kg^-1)
    "clay", # clay content (%)
    "sand", # sand content (%)
    "silt", # silt content (%)
    "ph.h2o", # pH in H2O
    "bdr", # bed rock depth (cm)
    "texture", # texture class
    "wpg2" # stone content (%)
  ),
  depth = 20,
  path = path_geodata
)

## 3. worldclim: https://www.worldclim.org/data/bioclim.html
worldclim_country(
  var = "bio",
  country = "MDG",
  res = 0.5
)

## 4. human footprint (either 1993 or 2009)
footprint(year = 2009) # It is expressed on a scale of 0 (low) to 50 (high footprint)

We will match the resolution and extent of all layers. Then match the environmental layers to capture Madagascar with terra::crop() and terra::mask().

# load the data from file (SpatVector)
# read administrative borders:
adm3 <-
  readRDS(
    here(path_geodata, "gadm", "gadm41_MDG_3_pk.rds")
  ) %>%
  select("NAME_1", "NAME_2", "NAME_3")


4.1.1 Cropping and Masking Rasters

# load the data from file (SpatRaster)

# read elevation:
elev <-
  rast(
    here(path_geodata, "elevation", "MDG_elv_msk.tif")
  ) %>%
  crop(., adm3) %>%
  mask(., adm3)
names(elev) <- "elevation"

# read soil:
soil <-
  rast(
    list.files(
      here(path_geodata, "soil_af_isda"),
      full.names = TRUE
    )
  ) %>%
  crop(., adm3) %>%
  mask(., adm3)

names(soil) <- c(
  "brd",
  "ctot",
  "clay",
  "oc",
  "ph",
  "sand",
  "silt",
  "texture",
  "stone"
)

# read climate:
bio <-
  rast(
    here(path_geodata, "climate", "wc2.1_country", "MDG_wc2.1_30s_bio.tif")
  ) %>%
  select("wc2.1_30s_bio_1", "wc2.1_30s_bio_12", "wc2.1_30s_bio_15") %>%
  crop(., adm3) %>%
  mask(., adm3)

climate <-
  c(
    bio$wc2.1_30s_bio_1, # annual temp
    bio$wc2.1_30s_bio_15, # precipiation seasonality
    bio$wc2.1_30s_bio_12 # annual prec
  )

names(climate) <- c("tavg", "prec_seas", "prec")

# footprint
footp <-
  rast(
    here(path_geodata, "landuse", "wildareas-v3-2009-human-footprint_geo.tif")
  ) %>%
  crop(., adm3) %>%
  mask(., adm3)
names(footp) <- "footp"

title: 5  Extract data from locations
text:
5.1 Extract data from grid cells
In this part we will extract different types of data from our geographical data (species records and environmental variables). We can do this to any kind of spatial data. Most commonly one would want to extract environmental data for certain locations (areas, grid cells, species occurrence points), or calculate some statistics on the species data over a certain area. Below are examples for both situations:

5.1.1 Species data (POINTS)

# our gbif data frame from script 02
gbif_dat <- readRDS(path_gbif)

# administrative borders of Madagascar from script 01
adm3 <- readRDS(path_adm)

We need to overlay a rectangular grid or administrative borders to calculate summary statistics for our gbif data across space.

adm_sf <-
  adm3 %>%
  select("NAME_1", "NAME_2", "NAME_3") %>%
  st_as_sf() %>%
  st_transform(crs = wkt_behrm) %>%
  mutate(
    area_type = "adm"
  )

Let’s create a grid. Below our cellsize is 50,000 m x 50,000 m ()

square_grid <- 
  st_make_grid(
    x = adm_sf,
    what = "polygons",
    cellsize = c(50000,50000)
  ) %>%
  st_sf(
    area_type = "cell",
    geom = .,
    cell_id = 1:length(.)
  )

sf_use_s2(FALSE)

Spherical geometry (s2) switched off

grid_50 <-
  square_grid %>%
  st_cast("POLYGON") %>%
  st_intersection(., adm_sf %>% select(geometry) %>% summarise()) %>%
  distinct() %>%
  st_make_valid()

Warning: attribute variables are assumed to be spatially constant throughout
all geometries

table(grid_50$area_type)


cell 
 294 

plot(grid_50["cell_id"])









5.1.1.1 Extract species records per grid cells
Merge species data and grid to the same sf object - we need to add the cell_id from the grid to our species data. since our species data is very large, we will reduce it first for computing SR and make it big afterwards again.

dat_sf <-
  gbif_dat %>%
  st_as_sf(
    coords = c("decimalLongitude", "decimalLatitude"),
    crs = "EPSG:4326"
  ) %>%
  st_transform(., crs = st_crs(grid_50))

dat_grid <-
  st_join(grid_50, dat_sf, join = st_intersects)

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = grid_50, fill = NA, color = "grey70") +
  geom_sf(data = dat_sf, color = "red", size = 0.5) +
  my_theme










5.1.1.2 Calculate species richness per grid
Here is where the cell_id we assigned earlier comes in handy. We can now group our data by cell id and sum up the number of records and distinct species per cell - giving us the species richness (SR) and record numbers (N).
Since many entries in GBIF are not determined to species-level, it might make sense to also calculate genus richness or family richness. However, this of course only makes sense when working with data from more than one genus.

SR <-
  dat_grid %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  group_by(cell_id) %>%
  summarise(
    N = sum(!is.na(gbifID)),
    SR = n_distinct(species, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    log_N = log(N),
    log_SR = log(SR)
  ) %>%
  right_join(grid_50) %>%
  st_as_sf()

Joining with `by = join_by(cell_id)`

plot(SR)

5.1.1.3 Plot species richness

p1 <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(
    data = SR,
    aes(fill = log_N),
    color = NA
  ) +
  geom_sf(
    data = grid_50,
    color = "lightgrey",
    size = 0.2,
    fill = NA
  ) +
  scale_fill_distiller(
    palette = "RdBu",
    limit = c(1, max(SR$log_N)),
    values = c(-1, 1),
    na.value = "darkgrey"
  ) +
  my_theme +
  labs(fill = "Species Records")


p2 <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(
    data = SR,
    aes(fill = log_SR),
    color = NA
  ) +
  geom_sf(
    data = grid_50,
    color = "lightgrey",
    size = 0.2,
    fill = NA
  ) +
  scale_fill_distiller(
    palette = "RdBu",
    limit = c(1, max(SR$log_SR)),
    values = c(-1, 1),
    na.value = "darkgrey"
  ) +
  my_theme +
  labs(fill = "Species Richness")


plot_grid(p1, p2, labels = c("A", "B"))











5.1.2 Environmental data
We can also extract our environmental data from the grid cells. For that we have to decide how we want to summarize the data within one grid cell to a single value. To keep it simple, let’s just average them for now.

env_stack_behrm <-
  readRDS(path_env)

We will compute our means directly on the raster stack but then convert the object into an sf-object for easier plotting and handling in general.

env_sf <- 
  env_stack_behrm %>%
  # compute mean env values per 50x50 km cell
  terra::extract(., grid_50, fun = mean, na.rm = TRUE) %>%
  # bind it back to gether with the cells
  cbind(grid_50, .) %>%
  # convert it back to sf
  st_as_sf()

# plot the gridded env data: for example elevation
plot(env_sf["elevation"])







# human footprint
plot(env_sf["footp"])







# soil organic carbon
plot(env_sf["oc"])

env_sf_long <- 
  env_sf %>% 
  pivot_longer(cols = 6:11) 

env_sf_long %>%
  ggplot()+
  geom_sf(
    data = env_sf_long, aes(fill = value), 
    color = NA) +
  geom_sf(
    data = grid_50,
    color = "lightgrey",
    size = 0.2,
    fill = NA) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "YlGnBu") +
  facet_wrap(~ name)+
  my_theme

env_sr_dat <- 
  env_sf %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  full_join(SR)

Now we have to prepare our spatial test. For this we need to prepare a couple of objects: - Definition of neighbors - Build neighborhood matrix - Assign spatial weights to the neighborhood matrix

# we define neighbors using k (the 5 closest neighbors)
knn <- knearneigh(sr_coords, k = 1)

# create the neighborhood matrix
nb <- knn2nb(knn)

Warning in knn2nb(knn): neighbour object has 45 sub-graphs

# deine spatial weights matrix
lw <- nb2listw(nb, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)

Now we can model Moran’s I which indicates spatial autocorrelation. Moran’s I > 0 → nearby points have similar values Moran’s I < 0 → nearby points are dissimilar Moran’s I ≈ 0 → random spatial pattern

# model moran's I for some example variables:

moran.test(
  sr_mod_dat$SR,
  lw
)

plot(
  cor_dat$correlation, 
  type="b", 
  pch=16, 
  cex=1.2,

Now let’s do the same for our model residuals.

# Correlogram for residuals
cor_res <- 
  correlog(
    sr_mod_dat$X,
    sr_mod_dat$Y,
    z=residuals(mod), 
    na.rm=T, 
    increment=50, 
    resamp=1, 
    latlon = TRUE)

Combine together: Black circles are our raw data and white are our model residuals. We would want them to be close to zero over the whole distance to be able to trust our model. We can see that the spatial signal from the autocorrelation in our response variable translates into the spatial signal of autocorrelation in our model residuals. This is because our simple model does not take into account the spatial structure of our data. There are other models that do (see below).
